listenings.text: Good morning, and welcome to the weekly metals report. Let's start with aluminum, which was the big story this week. The price soared by about six percent, its best week in two months. Two reasons. First, another smelter was closed in Europe because of electricity costs. Second, stocks in London warehouses have been falling for six weeks in a row. On the demand side, nothing has changed: orders from the energy sector are still very strong. So what is expected for next month? Most analysts think prices will stay high. But I'd be careful. This market has been very volatile, and one piece of news from China can change everything.

I'm the purchasing manager at a transformer factory near Lyon. For us, aluminum is not a detail, it is a big part of the cost of every transformer. So I keep an eye on the London price every morning, before anything else. Last year, when a new tariff was announced, we stockpiled metal for three months. It was expensive, and the warehouse was full, but it protected us when prices soared. Of course, we could not keep all the increase. We passed on about half of it to our clients. They were not happy, but they understood. Everybody in this industry knows the market is volatile.

Welcome, everybody. Our company is one of the bigger producers in China. About one million tons of aluminum are produced in our plants every year, and most of it is sold abroad. As you know, producing aluminum needs a lot of electricity. This year, a limit on energy use has been set in our region, so our production has been reduced by around ten percent. That is one reason prices are high right now. But please remember: this limit is being reviewed. If it is removed next year, there will be a surplus, and prices are expected to fall. So my advice to buyers is simple. Don't panic, and don't stockpile too much.

paras: Aluminum is one of the most traded commodities in the world. It is used in cars, cans, cables and the transformers that carry electricity to homes and factories. Its price is set every day on the London Metal Exchange, and over the last few years it has been unusually volatile: it soared in some months and plunged in others, sometimes by more than twenty percent.

Most of the world’s aluminum is produced in China, and producing it needs huge amounts of electricity. When energy prices rose in Europe, several smelters were closed, and a shortage was felt in many markets. At the same time, new tariffs were put on imported metal in some countries. Buyers who were afraid of higher prices stockpiled metal, which pushed prices up even further.

Demand is expected to keep growing, because aluminum is needed for electric cars, solar panels and new power networks. But a surplus in China could push prices down again. For companies that buy and sell the metal, the lesson is clear: the price cannot be controlled, so it has to be watched. Most of them keep an eye on the market every day and try to pass on only part of each increase to their clients.
